title: Connection Pooling Deep Dive
description: Learn how Redis connection pools work, when to tune them, and how to avoid exhaustion under high concurrency.

data.text: Establishing a TCP connection to Redis involves a handshake, authentication, and buffer allocation. Under high concurrency, creating a new connection per request is expensive and can exhaust file descriptors. Connection pooling solves this by maintaining a reusable set of open connections. Clients borrow a connection, execute commands, and return it to the pool instead of closing it.

A typical pool has a minimum size (connections kept warm), a maximum size (connections allowed in total), and an idle timeout (how long a connection can sit unused before being closed). When your application needs a connection, it borrows one from the pool. If all connections are busy and the pool is at maximum size, the request blocks until a connection is returned. This back-pressure prevents your application from overwhelming Redis with too many simultaneous requests.

data.text: The optimal pool size depends on your workload and Redis configuration. Redis is single-threaded per instance, so a pool larger than the number of CPU cores on the Redis server rarely helps. A common starting point is 2-4 connections per application instance, scaled by the number of application servers. For .NET applications using StackExchange.Redis, the default pool is 5 per endpoint; for Node.js ioredis, the default is 1.

data.text: If your code opens connections and never returns them to the pool, you will eventually hit the pool limit and block new requests. Always use using statements in C# or try-finally patterns in Node.js to ensure connections are returned.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Connection pooling eliminates per-request handshake overhead
Pool size should be tuned to workload, not maximized
Monitor wait times and utilization to catch leaks early
Keep-alive detects dead connections before they cause errors
data.takeaway: A well-tuned connection pool removes networking jitter from your Redis performance. Start with conservative sizes, monitor utilization, and scale only when metrics show contention.
